power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Participants. An a priori power analysis was conducted using G*Power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2009) for the cue type × deviation group interaction in a 3 × 2 mixed ANOVA, with cue type (positive, negative, neutral) as a within-subject factor and deviation group (15°, 35°) as a between-subject factor. Assuming a medium effect size (Cohen's f = 0.25), an alpha level of .05, and a statistical power of .80, a correlation of r = 0.5 among the three repeated measures, and a nonsphericity correction of ε = 1, the analysis indicated that a minimum total sample size of 28 participants (14 per group) was required. In Experiment 1A, we included 40 participants (28 female, 12 male, mean age =22.38 years, SD = 2.60) who were randomly assigned in equal numbers to the 15° and 35° groups (20 participants per group). Experiment 1B included an independent sample of 20 new participants (13 female, 7 male, mean age = 22.80, SD = 3.53), recruited from the same participant pool using the same eligibility criteria, matching the sample size of each deviation group in Experiment 1A. All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision; visual acuity and color vision were assured using an OCULUS Binoptometer 3 (OCULUS Optikgeräte GmbH, Wetzlar, Germany). Participants provided written informed consent before starting the experiment and they were compensated with either course credits or payment of 9€/hour. The study was approved by the ethics committee of the Department of Psychology at Philipps-Universität Marburg (No. 2021-56k) and conducted in accordance with the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki.

Participants. An a priori power analysis was conducted using G*Power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2009) for the cue deviation × cue direction interaction on positive cueing effects (positive minus neutral), which constituted our primary hypothesis test. This interaction was examined in a 6 × 2 mixed ANOVA, with cue deviation (3°, 12°, 24°, 36°, 48°, 60°) as a within-subject factor and cue direction (toward, away) as a between-subject factor. Assuming a medium effect size (Cohen's f = 0.25), an alpha level of .05, and a statistical power of .80, a correlation of r = 0.5 among the six repeated measures, and a nonsphericity correction of ε = 1, the analysis indicated that a minimum total sample size of 20 participants (10 per group) was required. Forty-two participants (37 female, 5 male, mean age = 22.60 years, SD = 3.09) took part in Experiment 2 and were randomly assigned in equal numbers to the toward-and away-cue groups (21 per groups). All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision. Visual acuity and color vision were assured using an OCULUS Binoptometer 3 (OCULUS Optikgeräte GmbH, Wetzlar, Germany). All participants provided written informed consent and were compensated with course credits or payment of 9€/hour. The study was approved by the ethics committee of the Department of Psychology at Philipps-Universität Marburg (No. 2021-56k) and conducted in accordance with the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki.

Performance did not differ significantly between the 15° (M = 0.03, SE = 0.23) and 35° (M = 0.06, SE = 0.21) deviation groups, F(1,38) = 0.01, p =.936, ηp² < 0.01.

table.text: Neither the cue type × group interaction, F(2,76) = 1.43, p =.245, ηp² = 0.04, nor the cue type × cue precision interaction, F(2,76) = 0.87, p =.424, ηp² =0.02, reached significance.
Neither the cue type × group interaction, F(2,76) = 1.43, p =.245, ηp² = 0.04, nor the cue type × cue precision interaction, F(2,76) = 0.87, p =.424, ηp² =0.02, reached significance.

The cue type × cue precision × group interaction reached significance F(2,76) = 3.49, p =.036, ηp² = 0.08, suggesting that the influence of cue precision on cueing effects varied with the cue deviation magnitude.
For the positive cueing effect, the cue precision × group interaction was significant, F(1, 38) = 7.60, p =.009, ηp² =0.17.

Planned contrasts showed that positive cueing effects did not differ between precise and imprecise cues in the 15°-deviation group, M diff = -0.19, SE = 0.16, t(19) =-1.16, p =.261, dz = -0.26, BF01 = 2.39; whereas it differed significantly in the 35°-deviation group, M diff = 0.58, SE = 0.22, t(19) = 2.57, p =.019, dz = 0.57, BF01 = 1/3.

This comparison was not significant, M diff = 0.08, SE = 0.15, t(19) = 0.55, p =.590, dz =0.12, BF01 = 3.76.

For negative cueing effects, the cue precision × group interaction was not significant, F(1,38) = 3.80, p =.059, ηp² = 0.09, providing insufficient evidence that the effect of cue precision differed between the two deviation groups.
In the 15°-deviation group, the negative cueing effects did not differ significantly between precise and imprecise cues, M diff = -0.25, SE = 0.20, t(19) = -1.25, p =.228, dz = -0.28, BF01 = 2.19.
Similarly, no significant difference was detected in the 35°deviation group, M diff = 0.35, SE = 0.23, t(19) = 1.50, p =.151, dz = 0.34, BF01 = 1.65.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 128 columns across 6 data files.
#### Issues Identified
2 file/column combinations have at least one issue.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 6 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Target-distractor color pairings in search displays varied across trials to discourage reliance on a single, consistently repeated target-distractor relation (Becker, 2010; Becker et al., 2013; Kerzel & Huynh Cong, 2024), and participants were instructed to use pre-cues to guide search.

Experiment 1B included an independent sample of 20 new participants (13 female, 7 male, mean age = 22.80, SD = 3.53), recruited from the same participant pool using the same eligibility criteria, matching the sample size of each deviation group in Experiment 1A.
All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision; visual acuity and color vision were assured using an OCULUS Binoptometer 3 (OCULUS Optikgeräte GmbH, Wetzlar, Germany).
Participants provided written informed consent before starting the experiment and they were compensated with either course credits or payment of 9€/hour.
Participants were seated in front of a 22-inch VPixx VIEWPixx monitor (Vpixx Technologies Inc.) at a viewing distance of approximately 100 cm.
Participants were instructed to search for a left-or right-tilted target embedded among seven chromatic distractors.
Prior to the main experiment, participants completed three practice blocks, one for each cue type, comprising 36 trials each.
All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
All participants provided written informed consent and were compensated with course credits or payment of 9€/hour.
Participants were encouraged to use the cues, and target-distractor pairings varied across trials so that a fixed feature relation could not reliably be learned.
Consent to participate: Informed consent was obtained from all individual participants included in the study.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 2 R code files.
#### Run order

No ordering signal (no data dependency, `source()` call, or numeric filename prefix) distinguishes the run order of these files. They may need to run in a specific order that could not be determined automatically — check this before running.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:2, File = c("AnalysisCodes.R", "AnalysisCodes_new.R"
), "Runs after" = c("—", "AnalysisCodes.R"), Basis = c("none", 
"dependency")), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 2 scripts: 1 ran without error, 1 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **1 script uses an object or function that only another script defines**, so in the second run that script was loaded first, in the same session: `AnalysisCodes_new.R` after `AnalysisCodes.R`. Such a script should `source()` the other itself, since it does not run on its own. 

*a script hit an `object '...' not found` error, indicating it expected a variable another script defines. We inferred which script supplies it and re-ordered so that script runs first, and re-ran once. The outcomes above are from that corrected run.*
**Undefined-variable errors**

**1 script failed on an undefined variable or function** (`object '...' not found` / `could not find function "..."`). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper's own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "AnalysisCodes_new.R", "Missing variable" = "plot1", 
    "Defined in" = "AnalysisCodes.R"), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**`setwd()` in the code**

**2 scripts call `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.
Reproducible after removing `setwd()`: AnalysisCodes.R.

info.title: When imprecise cues guide search: Direction-dependent effects of cue-feature mismatch

text.text: Informative pre-cues can guide visual search, but it remains unclear how precisely cue features must match the features they specify.
Across two experiments, we examined how cue-feature mismatch affected target-and distractor-based guidance.
Experiment 1 compared precise cues (0° deviation) with imprecise cues deviating by 15°, 35°, or 45° in separate groups.
Positive cues, indicating upcoming target features, reliably facilitated search, whereas negative cues, indicating upcoming distractor features, produced little benefit.
There was limited evidence that cueing effects changed specifically with cue precision.

Experiment 2 varied cue deviation from 3° to 60° within participants and manipulated cue direction, deviating toward or away from the competing feature (i.e. target or distractor), between two groups.
Positive cueing effects were direction-dependent, with large toward deviations reducing cueing benefits whereas away deviations left them unaffected.
However, away-shifted cues did not outperform the 3° reference, providing no direct evidence for optimally shifted attentional templates.
Negative cueing effects showed no reliable modulation by deviation magnitude or direction.
These findings indicate that target-based guidance can tolerate substantial cue-feature mismatch but is constrained by the cue's position relative to competing distractor features.
All data generated or analyzed during this research is available on the OSF repository: https://osf.io/fd6t3/.
text.formatted: All data generated or analyzed during this research is available on the OSF repository: <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/fd6t3/">https://osf.io/fd6t3/</ref>.

text.text: Visual search relies on the ability to direct attention toward task-relevant information while ignoring irrelevant distractors.

One key mechanism underlying this process involves setting up an attentional template (Duncan & Humphreys, 1989), a representation of task-relevant features that biases attentional selection (Desimone & Duncan, 1995; Wolfe, 1994 Wolfe, , 2021)).
text.formatted: One key mechanism underlying this process involves setting up an attentional template <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Duncan & Humphreys, 1989)</ref>, a representation of task-relevant features that biases attentional selection <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Desimone & Duncan, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Wolfe, 1994</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Wolfe, , 2021))</ref>.

text.text: Accumulating evidence indicates that such templates are not necessarily fixed but can be adjusted according to current search demands (Harris et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2022 Yu et al., , 2024)).
text.formatted: Accumulating evidence indicates that such templates are not necessarily fixed but can be adjusted according to current search demands <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Harris et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Yu et al., 2022</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Yu et al., , 2024))</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, feature information provided before search is not always perfectly precise.
The present study therefore asks how attentional guidance changes as the mismatch between an informative pre-cue and the feature it specifies increases.
Informative pre-cues can provide advance information about either a target or a distractor feature.

Positive cues provide information about the upcoming target and reliably facilitate visual search relative to non-informative or neutral cues (Arita et al., 2012; Beck et al., 2018; Beck & Hollingworth, 2015; Carlisle et al., 2011; Conci et al., 2019; Woodman et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2020 Zhang et al., , 2022;; Zhang & Carlisle, 2023).
text.formatted: Positive cues provide information about the upcoming target and reliably facilitate visual search relative to non-informative or neutral cues <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Arita et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Beck et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Beck & Hollingworth, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Carlisle et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Conci et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Woodman et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Zhang et al., 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Zhang et al., , 2022;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Zhang & Carlisle, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This benefit is attributed to target-based guidance, in which attention is biased toward items matching the target feature.
Negative cues provide information about features to be ignored and can also facilitate search.
This benefit is often attributed to distractor-based guidance, in which attention is biased away from items sharing the distractor feature.
However, the benefits of negative cues are typically smaller (Arita et al., 2012; Conci et al., 2019; Kerzel & Huynh Cong, 2022; Zhang et al., 2022; Zhang & Carlisle, 2023).
text.formatted: However, the benefits of negative cues are typically smaller <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Arita et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Conci et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Kerzel & Huynh Cong, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Zhang et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Zhang & Carlisle, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This difference raises the question of whether the two forms of guidance also differ in their sensitivity to the precision of advance feature information.
For target-based guidance, two theoretical accounts make different predictions about how such feature mismatch should affect attentional selection.

According to the feature-similarity gain account (Treue & Trujillo, 1999), attentional gain is maximal for features matching the currently relevant feature and decreases as feature similarity declines (Anderson & Folk, 2010; Ansorge & Becker, 2014).
text.formatted: According to the feature-similarity gain account <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Treue & Trujillo, 1999)</ref>, attentional gain is maximal for features matching the currently relevant feature and decreases as feature similarity declines <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Anderson & Folk, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Ansorge & Becker, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Applied to informative pre-cues, this account predicts that guidance should become progressively less effective as the cue differs more strongly from the feature it specifies.
A different prediction can be derived from the optimal tuning account (Navalpakkam & Itti, 2007).
text.formatted: A different prediction can be derived from the optimal tuning account <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Navalpakkam & Itti, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: This account was originally proposed for situations in which targets are difficult to discriminate from competing nontargets, predicting that attentional selection may be shifted away from distractor features rather than being centered on the veridical target feature (e.g., Becker, 2010; Geng et al., 2017; Navalpakkam & Itti, 2007; Yu & Geng, 2019).
text.formatted: This account was originally proposed for situations in which targets are difficult to discriminate from competing nontargets, predicting that attentional selection may be shifted away from distractor features rather than being centered on the veridical target feature (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Becker, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Geng et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Navalpakkam & Itti, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Yu & Geng, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, when searching for an orange target among yellower nontargets, attentional selectivity may be tuned toward a redder value because this increases target-distractor discriminability.

Such asymmetric tuning has been observed in some visual search studies, although evidence remains mixed and appears to depend on trial history (Becker, 2010; Becker et al., 2013 Becker et al., , 2014;; Chapman et al., 2023; Grössle et al., 2023; Hamblin-Frohman & Becker, 2021; Kerzel & Huynh Cong, 2024; Scolari & Serences, 2009; Scolari et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Such asymmetric tuning has been observed in some visual search studies, although evidence remains mixed and appears to depend on trial history <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Becker, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Becker et al., 2013</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Becker et al., , 2014;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Chapman et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Grössle et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Hamblin-Frohman & Becker, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Kerzel & Huynh Cong, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Scolari & Serences, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Scolari et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Extending this logic to informative pre-cues, attentional guidance may depend not only on the magnitude of cue-target mismatch, but also on whether the cued feature is displaced toward or away from the distractor.

Specifically, optimal tuning predicts that a cue shifted away from the distractor should outperform a cue that exactly matches the target feature, because such a cue allows observers to set up a template with greater target-distractor discriminability.
Conversely, a cue shifted toward the distractor should reduce the discriminability and thus impair performance.
Consequently, a deviation of the same magnitude should be less costly when it shifts the cued feature away from the distractor than when it shifts it toward the distractor.
Previous studies have used the contingent capture paradigm (Folk et al., 1992; Folk & Remington, 1998) to test predictions relevant to these two accounts.
text.formatted: Previous studies have used the contingent capture paradigm <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Folk et al., 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Folk & Remington, 1998)</ref> to test predictions relevant to these two accounts.

text.text: In such paradigms, spatially non-predictive peripheral cues serve as probes of the currently active attentional set and reveal which features are capable of triggering shifts of spatial attention (Anderson & Folk, 2010; Ansorge & Becker, 2014; Kerzel & Huynh Cong, 2024).
text.formatted: In such paradigms, spatially non-predictive peripheral cues serve as probes of the currently active attentional set and reveal which features are capable of triggering shifts of spatial attention <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Anderson & Folk, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Ansorge & Becker, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Kerzel & Huynh Cong, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The present study tested these predictions in a different cue-use context, in which feature cues were informative about the upcoming search and could therefore be used to guide subsequent selection.
Specifically, we asked whether guidance based on informative pre-cues varied primarily with the magnitude of cue-feature mismatch or also with its direction relative to competing features.
To resolve the question, we manipulated cue deviation across a broad range in a continuous color space.
Cue deviation was defined as the angular distance between the cue color and the feature specified by that cue.
For positive cues, this was the distance between the cue color and the upcoming target color; for negative cues, it was the distance between the cue color and the upcoming distractor color.
Smaller angular deviations therefore indicated more precise cue information.
Neutral cues indicated a color absent from the search display and were manipulated in parallel to provide deviationspecific baselines for measuring positive and negative cueing effects.
Cue direction was defined relative to the competing feature.
Positive-cue deviations were directed either toward or away from the distractor color, whereas negative-cue deviations were directed either toward or away from the target color.

Target-distractor color pairings in search displays varied across trials to discourage reliance on a single, consistently repeated target-distractor relation (Becker, 2010; Becker et al., 2013; Kerzel & Huynh Cong, 2024), and participants were instructed to use pre-cues to guide search.
text.formatted: Target-distractor color pairings in search displays varied across trials to discourage reliance on a single, consistently repeated target-distractor relation <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Becker, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Becker et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Kerzel & Huynh Cong, 2024)</ref>, and participants were instructed to use pre-cues to guide search.

text.text: The "feature-similarity gain" account (Treue & Trujillo, 1999) predicts that positive cueing benefits should decrease as cue-target deviation increases, with comparable reductions for toward and away deviations of the same magnitude.
text.formatted: The "feature-similarity gain" account <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Treue & Trujillo, 1999)</ref> predicts that positive cueing benefits should decrease as cue-target deviation increases, with comparable reductions for toward and away deviations of the same magnitude.

text.text: In contrast, the optimal tuning account (Navalpakkam & Itti, 2007) predicts that equally large deviations should produce better guidance when they shift the cue away from rather than toward the distractor, with an away-shifted cue outperforming the exact targetmatching reference providing stronger evidence for this account.
text.formatted: In contrast, the optimal tuning account <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Navalpakkam & Itti, 2007)</ref> predicts that equally large deviations should produce better guidance when they shift the cue away from rather than toward the distractor, with an away-shifted cue outperforming the exact targetmatching reference providing stronger evidence for this account.

text.text: The competing predictions of feature-similarity gain and optimal tuning primarily concern target-based guidance.
Negative cues provide a complementary test of whether distractor-based guidance is similarly sensitive to the magnitude and direction of cue-feature mismatch.
Experiment 1 examined whether cue-feature mismatch affected positive and negative cueing effects.
Within each deviation group, participants received both precise (0°) cues and cues that deviated from the feature they specified, allowing the 0° condition to serve as a within-participant reference.
Experiment 1A tested 15° and 35° deviations in separate participant groups, whereas Experiment 1B tested a 45° deviation in an independent sample.
This design allowed us to assess the effect of cue imprecision across different degrees of cue-feature mismatch.
Participants.

An a priori power analysis was conducted using G*Power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2009) for the cue type × deviation group interaction in a 3 × 2 mixed ANOVA, with cue type (positive, negative, neutral) as a within-subject factor and deviation group (15°, 35°) as a between-subject factor.
text.formatted: An a priori power analysis was conducted using G*Power 3.1 <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Faul et al., 2009)</ref> for the cue type × deviation group interaction in a 3 × 2 mixed ANOVA, with cue type (positive, negative, neutral) as a within-subject factor and deviation group (15°, 35°) as a between-subject factor.

text.text: Assuming a medium effect size (Cohen's f = 0.25), an alpha level of .05, and a statistical power of .80, a correlation of r = 0.5 among the three repeated measures, and a nonsphericity correction of ε = 1, the analysis indicated that a minimum total sample size of 28 participants (14 per group) was required.
In Experiment 1A, we included 40 participants (28 female, 12 male, mean age =22.38 years, SD = 2.60) who were randomly assigned in equal numbers to the 15° and 35° groups (20 participants per group).

Experiment 1B included an independent sample of 20 new participants (13 female, 7 male, mean age = 22.80, SD = 3.53), recruited from the same participant pool using the same eligibility criteria, matching the sample size of each deviation group in Experiment 1A.
All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision; visual acuity and color vision were assured using an OCULUS Binoptometer 3 (OCULUS Optikgeräte GmbH, Wetzlar, Germany).
Participants provided written informed consent before starting the experiment and they were compensated with either course credits or payment of 9€/hour.
The study was approved by the ethics committee of the Department of Psychology at Philipps-Universität Marburg (No. 2021-56k) and conducted in accordance with the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki.
The experiment was conducted in a dimly lit room with attenuated sound.
Participants were seated in front of a 22-inch VPixx VIEWPixx monitor (Vpixx Technologies Inc.) at a viewing distance of approximately 100 cm.
The experiment was controlled by a Windows 7 operating system (1680 x 1050 pixels, 60 Hz refresh rate) using E-Prime 2.0 software.
All stimuli were presented on a black (0.28cd/m²) background.
Each search display contained 24 Gabor patches, with patch radius of 0.81° of visual angle, defined by a cosine envelope with a spatial frequency of 0.05 and a standard deviation of 12 pixels.
All patches were generated using the online Gabor-patch generator (https://www.cogsci.nl/gabor-generator).
text.formatted: All patches were generated using the online Gabor-patch generator (<ref type="url" target="https://www.cogsci.nl/gabor-generator">https://www.cogsci.nl/gabor-generator</ref>).

text.text: The 24 Gabor patches were arranged on three imaginary circles (see Fig. 1A): 4 items on an inner circle (radius = 2.42°), 8 on a middle circle (radius = 4.84°) and 12 on an outer circle (radius = 7.26°).
text.formatted: The 24 Gabor patches were arranged on three imaginary circles (see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1A</ref>): 4 items on an inner circle (radius = 2.42°), 8 on a middle circle (radius = 4.84°) and 12 on an outer circle (radius = 7.26°).

text.text: Items were evenly spaced along each circle.
The colors used in the experiments were matched for luminance and defined in the CIELAB color space.
This color space is approximately perceptually uniform, such that equal distances in the space correspond to similar perceptual differences.

Each search display consisted of 16 task-irrelevant gray Gabor patches (L* = 70, a* = 0, b* = 0, where L* represents perceived lightness, a* indexes the redgreen axis, and b* indexes the yellow-blue axis) and 8 chromatic Gabor patches.
The gray patches were randomly assigned one of four orientations (horizontal/0°, vertical/90°, or ± 15° relative to vertical midline).
The 8 chromatic patches were task-relevant, consisting of 4 patches in the target color and 4 in a distractor color.

These colors were pseudo-randomly sampled from three equidistant hues (separated by 120°): red (L* = 70, a* = 40, b* = 0), green (L* = 70, a* = -20, b* = 34.60), and blue (L* = 70, a* = -20, b* = -34.60), with the constraint that each color was used equally often across trials.
To prevent a fixed target-distractor relation, the distractor hue varied relative to the target across trials (e.g., green or blue distractors for a red target).
The target was defined as the chromatic Gabor patch tilted either left (-15°) or right (+15°) relative to the vertical midline.
To prevent orientation-based pop-out, the achromatic nontarget patches were presented in heterogeneous orientations, substantially reducing the uniqueness of the target's orientation.
Variation in the orientations of the chromatic nontarget patches further increased orientation heterogeneity.

The target was never placed on the outer circle but appeared with equal probability at any of the remaining candidate locations on the inner and middle circles, thereby limiting the range of target eccentricities.
As shown in Fig. 1B, the cue display consisted of two circles (radius 0.69°) presented 1.62° to the left and right from the central fixation (see also Conci et al., 2019).
text.formatted: As shown in Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1B</ref>, the cue display consisted of two circles (radius 0.69°) presented 1.62° to the left and right from the central fixation (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Conci et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: On each trial, one of the circles was gray and the other was filled with a chromatic color (e.g., red, green or blue) that served as the cue.
The symbol presented at the circle center indicated the cue type: positive (+), negative (-), or neutral (o).

A positive (+) cue indicated the upcoming target color; a negative (-) cue color indicated the to-be-ignored distractor color, and a neutral cue (o) showed a color that did not appear in the subsequent search display.

Cue precision (see Fig. 1C) was defined as the angular deviation of the cue color from the relevant reference color (i.e., the actual target color for positive cues, the actual distractor color for negative cues, and the "absent" color for neutral cues) in the CIELAB a-b plane.
text.formatted: Cue precision (see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1C</ref>) was defined as the angular deviation of the cue color from the relevant reference color (i.e., the actual target color for positive cues, the actual distractor color for negative cues, and the "absent" color for neutral cues) in the CIELAB a-b plane.

text.text: Within each cue type, one-third of the trials were precise (0° deviation), and the remaining two-thirds were imprecise, with cue colors evenly deviating by ±15° in the high precision group (Experiment 1A), ±35° in the medium precision group (Experiment 1A), or ±45° in the low precision group (Experiment 1B).
The three deviations were selected on an exploratory basis.
All deviations stayed below 60°, corresponding to the midpoint between adjacent reference hues, at which the shifted cue would be equally compatible with either reference hue.
The selected values were intended to provide an initial sampling of different levels of cue imprecision rather than to test an independently established perceptual boundary.
Cue colors appeared equally often in each cue type, with the constraint that the color category (i.e., red, green, blue) did not repeat on consecutive trials.
Procedure and design.

As illustrated in Fig. 1D, each trial began with the presentation of a central fixation point accompanied by two arrow cues (length: 1.2°; positioned 0.8° above and below fixation), indicating the hemifield in which the task-relevant color would appear.
text.formatted: As illustrated in Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1D</ref>, each trial began with the presentation of a central fixation point accompanied by two arrow cues (length: 1.2°; positioned 0.8° above and below fixation), indicating the hemifield in which the task-relevant color would appear.

text.text: The arrows were retained from the paradigm used in previous studies (Conci et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2022) and allowed attention to be oriented to the position at which the chromatic cue would subsequently appear.
text.formatted: The arrows were retained from the paradigm used in previous studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Conci et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Zhang et al., 2022)</ref> and allowed attention to be oriented to the position at which the chromatic cue would subsequently appear.

text.text: Following a randomized delay of 300-500 ms, one of three cue types (positive, negative, or neutral) was presented for another 250 ms.
The left/right position of chromatic cue was counterbalanced and randomly intermixed, and the arrows identified that position in advance.
After another jittered delay of 800-1000 ms, the search display appeared.
Participants were instructed to search for a left-or right-tilted target embedded among seven chromatic distractors.

Responses were by pressing the left button with their right index finger for left-tilted targets, and the right button with their right middle finger for right-tilted targets on a gamepad as quickly and accurately as possible.
Incorrect or slow responses exceeding 4000 ms were followed by a feedback screen ("incorrect" or "too slow" in German) presented for 500 ms.
Each trial concluded with a 1000 ms blank interval.
After each block, feedback on mean accuracy and mean response time was shown for 3000 ms.
Cue types were presented in separate blocks to minimize trial-by-trial switching between different cue-use strategies.
This allowed participants to maintain the general strategy associated with each cue type.
Their order followed a Latin-square design and was counterbalanced across participants.
The experiment consisted of 12 blocks of 72 trials, resulting in a total of 864 trials.
Prior to the main experiment, participants completed three practice blocks, one for each cue type, comprising 36 trials each.
When calculating mean RTs, trials with responses faster than 200 ms or slower than 4000 ms were excluded.
Incorrect trials (which accounted for 2.40%-3.70% of trials) and trials with RTs exceeding ±2.5 SD from the condition-specific mean were also removed.
Accuracy, by contrast, was calculated across both correct and incorrect trials.

To account for potential speed-accuracy trade-offs, we evaluated overall performance using the Balanced Integration Score (BIS; Liesefeld et al., 2015; Liesefeld & Janczyk, 2019), which integrates RT and accuracy into a single score so that both measures are weighted equally in the assessment of performance.
text.formatted: To account for potential speed-accuracy trade-offs, we evaluated overall performance using the Balanced Integration Score (BIS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Liesefeld et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Liesefeld & Janczyk, 2019)</ref>, which integrates RT and accuracy into a single score so that both measures are weighted equally in the assessment of performance.

text.text: Higher (more positive) BIS values represent better performance.
To ensure results were comparable across groups, BIS values were calculated on the pooled data of all participants.
Statistical analyses were performed using JASP 0.18.3 (JASP Team, 2024).

Mean BIS values were submitted to a mixed ANOVA with cue type (positive, negative, neutral) and cue precision (precise, imprecise) as withinsubject factors and cue deviation group (15°, 35°) as a between-subject factor.
Statistical significance was defined as p < .05.
text.formatted: Statistical significance was defined as p < .05.

text.text: When the assumption of sphericity was violated, the Greenhouse-Geisser correction was applied.

Follow-up contrasts were conducted using paired-samples t-tests on participant-level condition means, with degrees of freedom determined as N -1. p values were Holm-adjusted for multiple comparisons, with the exception of the planned contrasts, which were not corrected.
Cohen's dz was calculated from the corresponding paired difference scores.
For all comparisons of theoretical interest, we additionally report BF01 values from Bayesian paired-samples t-tests, using a Cauchy prior with a default scale of r = 0.707.

Bayes factors were interpreted following Lee and Wagenmakers (2013): BF values of 1-3 were considered ₀₁ anecdotal evidence for the null hypothesis, 3-10 moderate, 10-30 strong, 30-100 very strong, and values above 100 extreme evidence.
text.formatted: Bayes factors were interpreted following <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Lee and Wagenmakers (2013)</ref>: BF values of 1-3 were considered ₀₁ anecdotal evidence for the null hypothesis, 3-10 moderate, 10-30 strong, 30-100 very strong, and values above 100 extreme evidence.

text.text: Correspondingly, BF values between 1/3 and 1 were considered anecdotal ₀₁ evidence for the alternative hypothesis, 1/10 -1/3 moderate, 1/30-1/10 strong, 1/100-1/30 very strong, and < 1/100 extreme evidence.
text.formatted: Correspondingly, BF values between 1/3 and 1 were considered anecdotal ₀₁ evidence for the alternative hypothesis, 1/10 -1/3 moderate, 1/30-1/10 strong, 1/100-1/30 very strong, and < 1/100 extreme evidence.

text.text: Experiment 1A.

Performance was the best for positive cues (M = 0.89, SE = 0.14), followed by negative (M = -0.38, SE = 0.18) and neutral cues (M = -0.39, SE = 0.17), reflected in a significant main effect of cue type, F(2,76) = 105.15, p <.001, ηp² = 0.74.
text.formatted: Performance was the best for positive cues (M = 0.89, SE = 0.14), followed by negative (M = -0.38, SE = 0.18) and neutral cues (M = -0.39, SE = 0.17), reflected in a significant main effect of cue type, F(2,76) = 105.15, p <.001, ηp² = 0.74.

text.text: Planned contrasts confirmed that positive cues produced better performance than neutral cues, t(39) = 12.38, p <.001, dz = 1.96, BF01 < 1/100, whereas negative and neutral cues did not differ, t(39)=0.10, p =.922, dz = 0.02, BF01 = 5.84.
text.formatted: Planned contrasts confirmed that positive cues produced better performance than neutral cues, t(39) = 12.38, p <.001, dz = 1.96, BF01 < 1/100, whereas negative and neutral cues did not differ, t(39)=0.10, p =.922, dz = 0.02, BF01 = 5.84.

text.text: Performance did not differ significantly between precise (M = 0.01, SE = 0.17) and imprecise (M = 0.07, SE = 0.15) cues, F(1,38) = 0.67, p =.417, ηp² = 0.02.
Performance did not differ significantly between the 15° (M = 0.03, SE = 0.23) and 35° (M = 0.06, SE = 0.21) deviation groups, F(1,38) = 0.01, p =.936, ηp² < 0.01.
text.formatted: Performance did not differ significantly between the 15° (M = 0.03, SE = 0.23) and 35° (M = 0.06, SE = 0.21) deviation groups, F(1,38) = 0.01, p =.936, ηp² < 0.01.

text.text: Neither the cue type × group interaction, F(2,76) = 1.43, p =.245, ηp² = 0.04, nor the cue type × cue precision interaction, F(2,76) = 0.87, p =.424, ηp² =0.02, reached significance.

The cue type × cue precision × group interaction reached significance F(2,76) = 3.49, p =.036, ηp² = 0.08, suggesting that the influence of cue precision on cueing effects varied with the cue deviation magnitude.
To decompose the three-way interaction, the cue precision × group interactions were tested separately for positive and negative cueing effects relative to neutral cues (see Fig. 2A).
text.formatted: To decompose the three-way interaction, the cue precision × group interactions were tested separately for positive and negative cueing effects relative to neutral cues (see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2A</ref>).

text.text: For the positive cueing effect, the cue precision × group interaction was significant, F(1, 38) = 7.60, p =.009, ηp² =0.17.

Planned contrasts showed that positive cueing effects did not differ between precise and imprecise cues in the 15°-deviation group, M diff = -0.19, SE = 0.16, t(19) =-1.16, p =.261, dz = -0.26, BF01 = 2.39; whereas it differed significantly in the 35°-deviation group, M diff = 0.58, SE = 0.22, t(19) = 2.57, p =.019, dz = 0.57, BF01 = 1/3.
To determine whether cue precision directly affected performance following positive cues, we compared precise and imprecise positive cue conditions in the 35°deviation group.
This comparison was not significant, M diff = 0.08, SE = 0.15, t(19) = 0.55, p =.590, dz =0.12, BF01 = 3.76.

Thus, although the positive cueing effects varied with cue precision in this group, the direct comparison within the positive cue condition provided no clear evidence that positive cue performance itself was modulated by cue precision.

For negative cueing effects, the cue precision × group interaction was not significant, F(1,38) = 3.80, p =.059, ηp² = 0.09, providing insufficient evidence that the effect of cue precision differed between the two deviation groups.
Nevertheless, because the effect of cue precision within each group was of theoretical interest, planned contrasts were conducted within the group.
In the 15°-deviation group, the negative cueing effects did not differ significantly between precise and imprecise cues, M diff = -0.25, SE = 0.20, t(19) = -1.25, p =.228, dz = -0.28, BF01 = 2.19.
Similarly, no significant difference was detected in the 35°deviation group, M diff = 0.35, SE = 0.23, t(19) = 1.50, p =.151, dz = 0.34, BF01 = 1.65.

The analysis revealed the highest performance for positive cues (M = 0.52, SE = 0.23), followed by neutral (M = -0.29, SE = 0.28) and negative (M = -0.49, SE = 0.34) cues, reflected in a significant main effect of cue type, F(2,38) = 22.44, p <.001, ηp² = 0.54.

text.text: Planned contrasts confirmed the benefit of positive cues over neutral cues, t(19) = 5.95, p <.001, dz = 1.33, BF01 < 1/100; whereas negative and neutral cues did not differ significantly, t(19) = -1.20, p =.247, dz = -0.27, BF01 = 2.31.
text.formatted: Planned contrasts confirmed the benefit of positive cues over neutral cues, t(19) = 5.95, p <.001, dz = 1.33, BF01 < 1/100; whereas negative and neutral cues did not differ significantly, t(19) = -1.20, p =.247, dz = -0.27, BF01 = 2.31.

text.text: Performance was better in the precise condition (M = 0.06, SE = 0.26) than in the imprecise condition (M = -0.23, SE =0.29), as indicated by a significant main effect of cue precision, F(1,19) = 12.34, p =.002, ηp² = 0.39.
However, the cue type × cue precision interaction was not significant, F(2,38) = 1.73, p =.192, ηp² = 0.08, providing insufficient evidence that the effect of cue precision differed across cue types.
Because precision-related changes in the positive and negative cueing effects were of direct theoretical interest, we conducted two theoretically motivated contrasts.
The positive cueing benefit did not differ significantly between precise and imprecise conditions, M diff = 0.08, SE = 0.21, t(19) = 0.40, p =.693, dz = 0.09, BF01 = 4.00.
Similarly, the negative cueing effect did not differ significantly between the two conditions, M diff = -0.37, SE = 0.31, t(19) = -1.17, p =.256, dz = -0.26, BF01 = 2.36 (see Fig. 2B).
text.formatted: Similarly, the negative cueing effect did not differ significantly between the two conditions, M diff = -0.37, SE = 0.31, t(19) = -1.17, p =.256, dz = -0.26, BF01 = 2.36 (see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2B</ref>).

text.text: Thus, neither cueing effects showed a statistically significant precision-related change.
Experiment 1 examined whether the effectiveness of positive and negative cues depended on how precisely the cue color matched its reference feature.
Across Experiments 1A and 1B, positive cues produced a robust benefit relative to neutral cues, whereas negative cues yielded little or no reliable benefit.
The precise cue condition provided a within-participant baseline for assessing the effect of cue precision.
In Experiment 1A, the precision-related change in the positive cueing effects differed between the 15°-and 35°-deviation groups.
Importantly, however, this interaction cannot be attributed straightforwardly to changes in target-based guidance.
In the 35° group, where the positive cueing effects differed between precise and imprecise cues, performance following positive cues themselves did not differ reliably with cue precision.
Instead, the change in the cueing effect was largely associated with variation in the neutral condition (see Table 1).
text.formatted: Instead, the change in the cueing effect was largely associated with variation in the neutral condition (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Thus, Experiment 1A provides little evidence that increasing cue-target mismatch up to 35° directly altered performance following positive cues.
In Experiment 1B, performance was generally better for precise than imprecise cues, but neither the positive nor the negative cueing effects showed a significant precision-related change.
Thus, the present findings provided limited evidence that target-or distractor-based guidance was specifically modulated by cue precision.
However, because the imprecise cue deviations were compared partly across independent samples, Experiment 1 provides limited evidence about how cueing effects change across these deviations.
Experiment 2 therefore manipulated cue deviation within participants over a broader range.
Experiment 1 provided robust positive cueing benefits but limited evidence that cue precision specifically modulated target-based attentional guidance.
One possibility is that the effect of cue precision depends on its direction relative to the competing feature.
That is, deviations toward and away from the distractor may have different consequences, which could be obscured when direction is not distinguished.
Experiment 2 therefore manipulated both cue deviation and cue direction.
Cue deviation was manipulated within participants, allowing the effect of deviation magnitude to be assessed within the same observers.
Cue direction was manipulated between participants so that each participant experienced a single, consistent mapping between cue deviation and the competing search feature throughout the experiment.

Intermixing toward and away cues within participants could have prevented template adjustment to a consistent deviation direction and introduced potential carryover effects between opposing cue-feature relations.
Because direction would be undefined at 0°, the smallest deviation was set at 3° to preserve formally distinct but closely matched toward and away conditions.

As the closest approximation to the reference color in the present design, the 3° condition was treated as a near-match reference, although its perceptual equivalence to an exact match was not directly tested.

The "feature-similarity gain" account (Treue & Trujillo, 1999) predicts that positive cueing benefits should decline relative to the 3° reference as cue-target deviation increases, with comparable reductions for toward and away deviations of the same magnitude.
text.formatted: The "feature-similarity gain" account <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Treue & Trujillo, 1999)</ref> predicts that positive cueing benefits should decline relative to the 3° reference as cue-target deviation increases, with comparable reductions for toward and away deviations of the same magnitude.

text.text: In contrast, the "optimal tuning" account (Navalpakkam & Itti, 2007) proposes that attentional templates are shifted away from distractor features to maximize target-distractor discriminability.
text.formatted: In contrast, the "optimal tuning" account <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Navalpakkam & Itti, 2007)</ref> proposes that attentional templates are shifted away from distractor features to maximize target-distractor discriminability.

text.text: It therefore predicts greater positive cueing benefits for cues that deviate away from, rather than toward, the distractor.
More critically, an a way cue outperforming the 3° reference would provide stronger evidence for optimal tuning than a directional asymmetry alone.
Negative cues were additionally included to assess whether distractorbased guidance exhibits similar sensitivity to deviation magnitude or direction.
Participants.

An a priori power analysis was conducted using G*Power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2009) for the cue deviation × cue direction interaction on positive cueing effects (positive minus neutral), which constituted our primary hypothesis test.
text.formatted: An a priori power analysis was conducted using G*Power 3.1 <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Faul et al., 2009)</ref> for the cue deviation × cue direction interaction on positive cueing effects (positive minus neutral), which constituted our primary hypothesis test.

text.text: This interaction was examined in a 6 × 2 mixed ANOVA, with cue deviation (3°, 12°, 24°, 36°, 48°, 60°) as a within-subject factor and cue direction (toward, away) as a between-subject factor.

Assuming a medium effect size (Cohen's f = 0.25), an alpha level of .05, and a statistical power of .80, a correlation of r = 0.5 among the six repeated measures, and a nonsphericity correction of ε = 1, the analysis indicated that a minimum total sample size of 20 participants (10 per group) was required.
Forty-two participants (37 female, 5 male, mean age = 22.60 years, SD = 3.09) took part in Experiment 2 and were randomly assigned in equal numbers to the toward-and away-cue groups (21 per groups).
All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
Visual acuity and color vision were assured using an OCULUS Binoptometer 3 (OCULUS Optikgeräte GmbH, Wetzlar, Germany).
All participants provided written informed consent and were compensated with course credits or payment of 9€/hour.
The study was approved by the ethics committee of the Department of Psychology at Philipps-Universität Marburg (No. 2021-56k) and conducted in accordance with the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki.
Apparatus, procedure and stimuli.

Apparatus, procedure, and stimuli were identical to those used in Experiment 1, except for the cue colors, which used a broader range of angular deviations from the reference color (±3°, ±12°, ±24°, ±36°, ±48°, ±60°).
Design.

In the toward group (see Fig. 3A), the cue color was shifted toward the distractor or target color (i.e., toward the distractor color with positive cues, toward the target color with negative or neutral cues).
text.formatted: In the toward group (see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3A</ref>), the cue color was shifted toward the distractor or target color (i.e., toward the distractor color with positive cues, toward the target color with negative or neutral cues).

text.text: In the away group (see Fig. 3B), the cue color was shifted away from the corresponding color.
text.formatted: In the away group (see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3B</ref>), the cue color was shifted away from the corresponding color.

text.text: Within each group, three levels of cue type (positive, negative, neutral) and six levels of cue deviation (3°, 12°, 24°, 36°, 48°, 60°) were used.
The experiment consisted of 18 blocks of 72 trials each, yielding a total of 1296 trials.
Each block contained 12 trials at each deviation level, randomly ordered, resulting in 72 trials per deviation for each cue type.
Behavioral pre-processing steps were identical to those used in Experiment 1.

Mean BIS values were submitted to a repeated-measures ANOVA with cue type (positive, negative, neutral) and cue deviation (3°, 12°, 24°, 36°, 48°, 60°) as within-subject factors and cue direction (toward, away) as a between-subject factor.
The Bayesian analysis approach was identical to that used in Experiment 1.
Mean RTs and error rates are reported in supplementary Table S3.
text.formatted: Mean RTs and error rates are reported in supplementary Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">S3</ref>.

text.text: We first compared the performance across cue types.

BIS was highest following positive cues (M = 0.49, SE = 0.17), followed by negative (M = -0.29, SE = 0.19) and neutral cues (M = -0.16, SE = 0.18), yielding a main effect of cue type, F(1.60, 63.82) = 35.93, p < .001, ηp² = 0.47.

text.text: Planned contrasts confirmed the benefit of positive cues over neutral cues, t(41) = 8.09, p <.001, dz = 1.25, BF01 < 1/100, whereas negative and neutral cues did not differ, t(41) = -1.41, p =.168, dz = -0.22, BF01 = 2.41.

text.text: In addition, the cue deviation × cue type interaction was also significant, F(10,400) = 2.67, p =.004, ηp² =.06, indicating that the influence of cue deviation on performance varied across cue types.

Crucially, the three-way interaction among cue deviation, cue type, and cue direction also reached significance (see Table 3), F(10, 400) = 2.13, p =.022, ηp² =.05, suggesting that the influence of cue deviation on cueing effects varied as a function of cue direction.

text.text: To decompose this three-way interaction, we separately analyzed positive and negative cueing effects.

Baseline-corrected BIS values (ΔBIS: positive/negative minus neutral) were submitted to two mixed ANOVAs, with cue deviation (3°, 12°, 24°, 36°, 48°, 60°) as a within-subject factor and cue direction (toward, away) as a between-subject factor.

For positive cueing effects, the main effect of cue deviation was significant, F(5, 200) = 4.39, p <.001, ηp² =0.10, and the main effect of cue direction was significant, F(1, 40) = 4.92, p =.032, ηp² =0.11.
text.formatted: For positive cueing effects, the main effect of cue deviation was significant, F(5, 200) = 4.39, p <.001, ηp² =0.10, and the main effect of cue direction was significant, F(1, 40) = 4.92, p =.032, ηp² =0.11.

text.text: Importantly, a significant interaction between cue deviation and direction also emerged (see Fig. 4A), F(5, 200) = 3.28, p =.007, ηp² =0.08, indicating that the effect of cue deviation on the positive cueing effects differed between the toward and away groups.
text.formatted: Importantly, a significant interaction between cue deviation and direction also emerged (see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4A</ref>), F(5, 200) = 3.28, p =.007, ηp² =0.08, indicating that the effect of cue deviation on the positive cueing effects differed between the toward and away groups.

text.text: For negative cueing effects, the main effect of cue deviation was not significant, F(5, 200) = 0.67, p =.649, ηp² =0.02, and neither was the main effect of cue direction, F(1, 40) = 0.42, p =.521, ηp² =0.01.
The cue deviation × cue direction interaction was not significant either (see Fig. 4B), F(5, 200) = 0.33, p =.892, ηp² <.01.
text.formatted: The cue deviation × cue direction interaction was not significant either (see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4B</ref>), F(5, 200) = 0.33, p =.892, ηp² <.01.

text.text: Thus, no significant direction-dependent change in the negative cueing effect was detected.
To characterize the cue deviation × cue direction observed for positive cueing effects, we examined how this effect changed relative to the 3° condition within each direction group.
Because Experiment 2 did not include an exact-match condition, the 3° condition, which had the smallest physical cuetarget deviation, was used as a near-match reference.
The five comparisons with the 3° reference were Holm-corrected within each cue-direction group.

As shown in Fig. 4A, in the away group, none of the positive cueing effects differed significantly from the 3° reference, M diff = -0.39 to 0.25, all ps Holm = 1.000, dz = -0.25 to 0.17, BF01 = 2.42 to 4.26.

text.text: Thus, reliable reductions relative to the near-match reference emerged only at the two largest toward deviations.

To determine whether these reductions in the toward group reflected poorer performance following positive cues or changes in the neutral cue condition, we compared BIS at each deviation with the 3° reference separately for positive and neutral cues.
Within each cue condition, the five comparisons with the 3° reference were Holm-corrected; only the theoretically relevant 48° and 60° comparisons are reported here.

In the positive cue condition, performance was significantly lower than 3° at both 48°, M diff = -0.73, SE = 0.18, t(20) = -4.01, p Holm =.003, dz = -0.88, BF01 = 1/50, and 60°, M diff = -1.24, SE = 0.18, t(20) = -7.02, p Holm <.001, dz = -1.53, BF01 < 1/100.
