text.text: In contrast, in the neutral cue condition, performance did not differ significantly from the 3° at either 48°, M diff = 0.01, SE = 0.22, t(20) = 0.06, p Holm =1.000, dz = 0.01, BF01 = 4.39, or 60°, M diff = 0.30, SE = 0.18, t(20) = 1.64, p Holm =.351, dz = 0.36, BF01 = 1.40.

Thus, the reductions in positive cueing effects at the two largest toward deviations were accompanied by lower BIS in the positive cue condition, whereas no statistically reliable differences were detected in the neutral cue condition. bars denote ±1 standard error of the mean.
Gray lines at the 0 on the y-axis denote the unified baseline.
Values above zero denote cueing benefits, while values below zero denote cueing costs.
In Experiment 2, positive cues again reliably facilitated search performance, whereas negative cues did not yield benefits relative to neutral cues, replicating the findings observed in Experiment 1.
Crucially, positive cueing effects varied as a function of both the magnitude and direction of cue deviation.
In the toward group, positive cueing effects remained comparable with the 3° reference at deviations up to 36° but was reduced at 48° and 60°.

Analyses of the constituent conditions indicated that these reductions were associated with poorer performance following positive cues rather than corresponding changes in the neutral baseline, consistent with the interpretation that large deviations toward the distractor impaired target-based guidance.
In contrast, positive cueing effects in the away group did not differ significantly from the 3° reference at any deviation.
Thus, the interaction was primarily attributable to reduced guidance for large toward deviations rather than enhanced guidance for away deviations.

This directional asymmetry is difficult to reconcile with a strict feature-similarity gain account (Treue & Trujillo, 1999), which would predict that performance is determined primarily by the magnitude of the cue-target difference, irrespective of its direction.
text.formatted: This directional asymmetry is difficult to reconcile with a strict feature-similarity gain account <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Treue & Trujillo, 1999)</ref>, which would predict that performance is determined primarily by the magnitude of the cue-target difference, irrespective of its direction.

text.text: The findings are broadly consistent with the idea that target-distractor relations constrain the effective range of target-based attentional guidance, as indicated by the optimal tuning account (Navalpakkam & Itti, 2007).
text.formatted: The findings are broadly consistent with the idea that target-distractor relations constrain the effective range of target-based attentional guidance, as indicated by the optimal tuning account <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Navalpakkam & Itti, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: However, because cues deviating away from the distractor did not outperform the 3° reference, the results do not provide direct evidence that attentional templates were optimally shifted away from the distractor.
Rather, they show that large cue deviations were especially detrimental when they shifted the cued feature toward the distractor.
Across two experiments, the present study examined how cue-feature mismatch constrains attentional guidance based on informative target and distractor information.
Positive cues consistently facilitated search performance relative to neutral cues, whereas negative cues did not produce reliable benefits.
The effects of cue precision, however, were less straightforward than a simple decline in performance with increasing deviations.
Experiment 1 provided limited evidence that cue precision specifically altered either positive or negative cueing effects.
Experiment 2 showed that larger deviations toward the distractor reduced positive cueing effects, whereas deviations away from the distractor did not produce a corresponding reduction.
Importantly, away-shifted cues also did not outperform the nearmatch reference condition.

Collectively, these results indicate that target-based guidance depends on the relation between the cued feature and competing distractor information, but they do not provide direct evidence that attentional templates are shifted to an optimally tuned feature value.
Experiment 1 showed robust positive cueing benefits across all deviation groups, but provided little evidence that these benefits were determined by cue precision.

In Experiment 1A, the precisionrelated change in the positive cueing effects differed between the 15°-and 35°-deviation groups, but the effect in the 35° group was largely attributable to variation in the neutral condition rather than to a reliable change in performance following positive cues themselves.
Experiment 1B likewise showed an overall advantage for precise over imprecise cues, but this effect did not reliably differ across cue types.
Experiment 2 leads to a similar conclusion for the smaller cue deviations.
Positive cueing effects did not show a systematic decline from 3° through 36°, and the numerical values fluctuated across these conditions rather than decreasing monotonically.
These results suggest that moderate discrepancies between the cue and target can still support effective attentional guidance.

This interpretation is consistent with proposals that the representation used to guide search need not preserve the target feature with the same fidelity required for subsequent target identification (Wilschut et al., 2014; Wolfe, 2021; Yu et al., 2022).
text.formatted: This interpretation is consistent with proposals that the representation used to guide search need not preserve the target feature with the same fidelity required for subsequent target identification <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Wilschut et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Wolfe, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Yu et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Coarse or category-consistent feature information may therefore remain useful even when the cue is not an exact physical match to the target (Daoutis et al., 2006; Wolfe, 2021).
text.formatted: Coarse or category-consistent feature information may therefore remain useful even when the cue is not an exact physical match to the target <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Daoutis et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Wolfe, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: We thank an anonymous reviewer for suggesting a discussion of the feature-based surround suppression (Störmer & Alvarez, 2014; see also Chapman et al., 2023) in Experiment 1 with exactmatch trials included.
text.formatted: We thank an anonymous reviewer for suggesting a discussion of the feature-based surround suppression (Störmer & Alvarez, 2014; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Chapman et al., 2023)</ref> in Experiment 1 with exactmatch trials included.

text.text: Such accounts predict enhanced processing of the attended feature itself but suppression of nearby features in feature space, with this suppression weakening as feature distance increases.
Accordingly, if feature-based attention was centered on the positive cue color, the target would coincide with this center at 0° but fall away from it under cue-target mismatch.
A small mismatch could therefore place the target within a suppressive surround, resulting in poorer performance than in the exact-match condition.
At larger cue-target distances, the target may move beyond the region of strongest suppression, in which case some recovery in performance would be expected.
We found no clear evidence for such a non-monotonic pattern.
Positive-cue performance at the 15° deviation was similar to that in the corresponding 0° condition, and no subsequent recovery was evident at the larger tested deviations.

However, because the present deviation levels were not selected to map the width of the suppressive surround and sampled feature space only sparsely, we cannot determine whether any of the tested deviations fell within the region of strongest suppression.
The present findings therefore neither provide clear support for nor a strong test of feature-based surround suppression.
Experiment 2 was designed to distinguish predictions based solely on cue-target similarity from predictions that additionally depend on the relation between target and distractor features.

A strict feature-similarity gain account predicts that performance should deteriorate as cue-target distance increases and that equally large deviations should have comparable consequences regardless of direction (Treue & Trujillo, 1999).
text.formatted: A strict feature-similarity gain account predicts that performance should deteriorate as cue-target distance increases and that equally large deviations should have comparable consequences regardless of direction <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Treue & Trujillo, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: The observed pattern did not conform to this simple prediction.
At large deviations (48° and 60°), positive cueing effects were reduced when the cue shifted toward the distractor, whereas away-shifted cues did not show a comparable reduction.
Thus, the consequences of cue-target mismatch appear to depend on the competing distractor feature, rather than on cuetarget similarity alone.
The 60° condition imposes an additional constraint on this interpretation.
At this deviation, positive and negative cues were identical in color in the toward group, whereas negative and neutral cues were identical in the away group.
Because this introduced a systematic difference between the two direction groups beyond cue direction itself, the 60° condition could confound the interpretation of directiondependent effects.

To assess whether the direction-dependent modulation of cueing effects depended on the ambiguous 60° condition, we repeated the analyses of positive and negative cueing effects after excluding this deviation (see Supplementary Materials).

The cue deviation × cue direction interaction for positive cueing effects remained significant in both BIS and RT, whereas the corresponding interaction for negative cueing effects remained non-significant.

This indicates that the directional modulation of positive cueing effects was not solely driven by the cue-color overlap at 60°, although the 60° condition itself remains difficult to interpret because of its structural ambiguity.
Importantly, a reduced positive cueing effect was already evident at the 48° toward deviation, where cue colors remained physically distinct.
This indicates that detrimental effects of shifting the cue toward the distractor can emerge before the structural ambiguity introduced at 60° is reached.
However, this directional asymmetry should not be equated with direct evidence for optimal tuning (Navalpakkam & Itti, 2007).
text.formatted: However, this directional asymmetry should not be equated with direct evidence for optimal tuning <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Navalpakkam & Itti, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: The optimal tuning account predicts that shifting the guiding representation away from distractors can increase target-distractor discriminability.
Deviations shifting the cued feature away from the distractor should therefore be less detrimental than those shifting it toward the distractor.
A particularly diagnostic prediction is that an away-shifted cue should outperform a cue that (nearly) matches the target.
In Experiment 2, however, none of the away conditions reliably exceeded the 3° near-match reference.
The present results therefore showed that large deviations toward the distractor are especially detrimental, but not that attentional templates were optimally shifted away from the distractor.

Nonetheless, target-based guidance can tolerate substantial deviations from the target feature without additional costs relative to the near-match reference, provided that the deviation shifts the cue away from the distractor.

This pattern is broadly compatible with a key premise of optimal tuning, whereby the influence of an imprecise template depends on its position relative to the distractor, rather than solely on its distance from the target.

A related consideration is that the behavioral patterns predicted by "optimal tuning" (Navalpakkam & Itti, 2007) are often mirrored by "relational" (Becker, 2010) accounts, despite their mechanistic divergence.
text.formatted: A related consideration is that the behavioral patterns predicted by "optimal tuning" <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Navalpakkam & Itti, 2007)</ref> are often mirrored by "relational" <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Becker, 2010)</ref> accounts, despite their mechanistic divergence.

text.text: For instance, when searching for an orange target among yellower distractors, the target is consistently redder than the distractors; consequently, nontargets (e.g., red) sharing this relational direction can capture attention, mimicking the appearance of an adaptive shift away from distractor features.

This convergence has led these accounts to be frequently considered together in the literature (Becker et al., 2014; Kerzel, 2020; Yu et al., 2022), especially in designs with consistent targetdistractor relations (Becker, 2010; Becker et al., 2013).
text.formatted: This convergence has led these accounts to be frequently considered together in the literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Becker et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Kerzel, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Yu et al., 2022)</ref>, especially in designs with consistent targetdistractor relations <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Becker, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Becker et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: The relational account (Becker, 2010) assumes that attentional guidance can rely on relations that generalize across trials.
text.formatted: The relational account <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Becker, 2010)</ref> assumes that attentional guidance can rely on relations that generalize across trials.

text.text: Because target-distractor direction varied across trials in the present study, participants could not rely on a fixed directional rule.
However, all target-distractor pairs were separated by the same 120° distance in color space, leaving open a more abstract relational strategy.

For example, participants could select the search color closer to a positive cue, a relation that becomes less discriminative as a toward cue approaches the midpoint between target and distractor but remains informative for away cues.
Such a strategy could therefore produce the observed direction-dependent modulation without requiring an optimally shifted feature template.
The present design thus cannot fully distinguish feature-specific tuning from more abstract relational guidance.
What can be concluded from the negative cues?

Across both experiments, negative cues produced little or no reliable benefit relative to neutral cues, and we found no reliable evidence that negative cueing effects varied systematically with cue deviation or direction.
These findings contrast with studies in which negative cues have facilitated search (Arita et al., 2012; Conci et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2022; Zhang & Carlisle, 2023).
text.formatted: These findings contrast with studies in which negative cues have facilitated search <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Arita et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Conci et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Zhang et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Zhang & Carlisle, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: One possibility is that the null effects simply reflect insufficient statistical power or inadequate sensitivity to detect precision-related changes.
However, this explanation is unlikely for several reasons.
First, the feature-based search task was comparable to those used in studies that robustly demonstrated negative cueing effects (Arita et al., 2012; Conci et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2022).
text.formatted: First, the feature-based search task was comparable to those used in studies that robustly demonstrated negative cueing effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Arita et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Conci et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Zhang et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Both experiments included substantial trial counts per condition and sample sizes similar to those in which optimal tuning has been observed (Yu et al., 2022; Yu & Geng, 2019).
text.formatted: Both experiments included substantial trial counts per condition and sample sizes similar to those in which optimal tuning has been observed <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Yu et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Yu & Geng, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, negative cues were structurally equivalent to positive cues and provided the same amount of information; variability in negative cue trials was not appreciably higher than in positive cue trials.
These considerations suggest that the design had sufficient power to detect precision-related effects, had they been present.

Nevertheless, the associated Bayes factors were generally inconclusive, providing at most anecdotal evidence and no consistent support for either the presence or absence of precision-related modulation.
We therefore cannot draw firm conclusions regarding negative cueing effects from the present data.
Future studies in which negative cues provide stronger or more consistent utility will be needed to determine whether distractor-based representations themselves can be flexibly tuned.
Another possibility is that the present task favored target-based guidance.
The observer's ultimate task was always to identify a predefined target, and positive cues mapped directly onto the feature that could guide selection of that target.

Negative cues instead specified a feature to be rejected and therefore required observers to use the cue indirectly to constrain the remaining candidate features, which may simply be a less efficient strategy.

Besides, studies reporting reliable negative cueing effects (Arita et al., 2012; Conci et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2022; Zhang & Carlisle, 2023) typically employed cues that perfectly matched the distractor feature, thereby maintaining high utility.
text.formatted: Besides, studies reporting reliable negative cueing effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Arita et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Conci et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Zhang et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Zhang & Carlisle, 2023)</ref> typically employed cues that perfectly matched the distractor feature, thereby maintaining high utility.

text.text: In the present study, however, cue-feature mismatch was manipulated such that imprecise cues constituted the majority of trials.
This reduced reliability may have discouraged participants from investing in maintenance of a distractor-based attentional template.

Furthermore, since negative cueing benefits have been shown to emerge only under high task demands (Conci et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2022), the current task may have been too easy for negative cues to serve as an effective strategy.
text.formatted: Furthermore, since negative cueing benefits have been shown to emerge only under high task demands <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Conci et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Zhang et al., 2022)</ref>, the current task may have been too easy for negative cues to serve as an effective strategy.

text.text: If the effort required to maintain a distractor representation outweighs its expected benefit, observers may use negative cues inconsistently or disregard them altogether.
This interpretation is compatible with evidence that strategic cue use depends strongly on both exact and expected task demands (Conci et al., 2019; Kerzel & Huynh Cong, 2022; Han et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This interpretation is compatible with evidence that strategic cue use depends strongly on both exact and expected task demands <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Conci et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Kerzel & Huynh Cong, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Han et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The present task differs from paradigms such as contingent capture (Folk et al., 1992; Folk & Remington, 1998; Kerzel, 2019 Kerzel, , 2020 Kerzel, , 2025)), in which cues are brief and explicitly non-predictive.
text.formatted: The present task differs from paradigms such as contingent capture <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Folk et al., 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Folk & Remington, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Kerzel, 2019</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Kerzel, , 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Kerzel, , 2025))</ref>, in which cues are brief and explicitly non-predictive.

text.text: These cues serve as diagnostic probes that reveal which features are capable of automatically attracting attention given the current attentional set.
In contrast, the present study was designed to examine how observers use informative pre-cues to prepare for search.
Participants were encouraged to use the cues, and target-distractor pairings varied across trials so that a fixed feature relation could not reliably be learned.
These design features increase the relevance of cue information for search, although they do not imply that the cue use was exclusively voluntary.

The present findings should therefore be understood as characterizing attentional guidance based on informative pre-cues rather than as establishing a strict dichotomy between voluntary and involuntary attention.

Besides, because cue types were blocked in the present study, participants may have maintained a general target-or distractor-based guidance strategy while updating the specific color information provided by each cue.
Whether comparable effects emerge when cue types are intermixed remains an open question.

In sum, the present study shows that the benefits of positive cues depend not only on how closely they match the target, but also on how the cued feature is positioned relative to competing distractor features.
This directional dependence is not readily explained by cue-target similarity alone, although the present results do not uniquely identify an optimally shifted attentional template.
Negative cues, in contrast, produced little reliable benefit under the present task conditions and showed no reliable modulation by cue deviation or direction.

text.text: Overall, the principal BIS pattern was primarily driven by response speed rather than accuracy.
At the 60° deviation, positive and negative cues were identical in color in the toward group, whereas negative and neutral cues were identical in the away group.
Because this introduced a systematic difference between the two direction groups beyond cue direction itself, the 60° condition could confound the interpretation of direction-dependent effects.

We therefore excluded this condition and repeated the analyses of positive and negative cueing effects to determine whether their modulation by cue direction remained evident across the deviation range unaffected by cue color overlap.

Baseline-corrected cueing effects (ΔBIS: positive/negative minus neutral) were each submitted to separate mixed ANOVAs with cue deviation (3°, 12°, 24°, 36°, 48°) as a within-subject factor and cue direction (toward, away) as a between-subject factor.
For positive cueing effects, the cue deviation × cue direction interaction was significant, F(4, 160) = 2.50, p =.045, ηp² = 0.06.
Followup contrasts among the remaining deviation levels relative to the 3° reference yielded the same results as those reported in the main text.
For negative cueing effects, the corresponding interaction was not significant, F(4, 160) = 0.39, p =.814, ηp² = 0.01.
The same analyses were conducted on RT-and error-rate-based positive and negative cueing effects.

For RTs, cue deviation × cue direction interaction was significant for positive cueing effects, F(2.64, 105.65) = 3.47, p =.023, ηp² = 0.08, but not for negative cueing effects, F(3.15, 125.98) = 0.54, p =.662, ηp² = 0.01.

The corresponding interaction in error rates was not significant for either positive cueing effects, F(4, 160) = 1.64, p =.166, ηp² = 0.04, or negative cueing effects, F(4, 160) = 0.39, p =.814, ηp² = 0.01.

Figure 1.
Stimuli arrangement and example trial sequence.
(A) Example visual search display.
Eight colored Gabor patches were presented among 16 gray Gabor patches four patches are rendered in the target color (e.g., red), four in the distractor color (e.g., green).
The dashed circle (not shown on the experiment) denotes the location of the target.
For illustration purposes, the background color was changed to dark gray to improve color visibility in this graph.
(B) Illustration of cue display.

The positive (+) cue indicated the color of the target set (i.e., TC), the negative (-) cue indicated the color of the distractor set (i.e., DC), and the neutral (o) cue indicated a color that did not appear in the search display (i.e., AC).
(C) Illustration of cue color assignment.
Positive cues reference the target color (TC); negative cues the distractor color (DC); and neutral cues to an absent color (AC).
Cue colors were shifted by ±15°, ±35°, or ±45° in separate groups.
(D) An example trial sequence.
Each trial started with an arrow cue that indicated the side on which the task-relevant color cue appeared.
After a short delay (300-500 ms), either a positive, a negative or a neutral cue was presented for 250 ms.

After another delay (800-1000 ms), the search display was shown, which required participants to detect an orientation target (highlighted with a dashed white circle) and report whether its orientation was tilted to the left or right.
Stimuli are not drawn to scale.
Figure 2.
ΔBIS results in Experiment 1.
ΔBIS was calculated by subtracting the BIS values of the neutral cue condition from those of the positive and negative cue conditions.
(A) Results for Experiment 1A, comparing 15°-deviation (left) and 35°-deviation (right) groups.
(B) Results for Experiment 1B, showing the 45°-deviation group.
Bars denote group means with ±1 standard error of the mean.
Blue bars denote positive cues, orange bars denote negative cues, dark colors denote precise cues, light colors denote imprecise cues, and gray lines serves as the zero-baseline.
Dots denote individual participants, with lines connecting performance of single participants.
Dot colors denote group membership.
Figure 3.
Illustration of cue directions shifting toward (A) and away from (B) the target-distractor relation.

(A)In the toward direction, positive cue colors were shifted toward the distractor color (i.e., DC), and negative cue colors were shifted toward the target color (i.e., TC), and neutral cue colors were shifted toward the target color (i.e., TC).

(B) In the away direction, positive cue colors were shifted away from the distractor color (i.e., DC), and negative cue colors were shifted away from the target color (i.e., TC), and neutral cue colors were shifted away from the target color (i.e., TC).
Figure 4.
Results of Experiment 2.

(A) ΔBIS (positive minus neutral) as a function of cue deviation (3°, 12°, 24°, 36°, 48°, 60°), shown for cue directions shifting toward and away from the target-distractor relation; (B) ΔBIS (negative minus neutral) as a function of cue deviation; the graph follows the same logic as in (A).
